questions.stem: What is the main weakness of one-hot encoding for representing words?
choices: It cannot represent more than 1,000 words
Every word is equidistant from every other, so it encodes no similarity, and the vectors are as long as the vocabulary
It requires a GPU
It cannot be used with neural networks
questions.explanation: One-hot vectors are orthogonal by construction: 'cat' is exactly as far from 'dog' as from 'parliament'. They also grow with the vocabulary, producing enormous sparse inputs. Both problems are what dense embeddings were introduced to solve.

questions.stem: What does a bag-of-words representation discard?
choices: The identity of the words
Word order and syntax, keeping only which words occur and how often
The document length
The vocabulary
questions.explanation: Bag of words records counts and throws away sequence, so 'the dog bit the man' and 'the man bit the dog' are identical. That makes it fast and surprisingly effective for topic-level tasks, and useless where order carries the meaning.

questions.stem: What property do word embeddings have that one-hot vectors lack?
choices: They are longer
Semantically related words occupy nearby positions in a continuous vector space
They are binary
They require no training
questions.explanation: Embeddings are learned dense vectors in which distance reflects distributional similarity, so related words cluster. That geometry is what lets a model generalise from a word it saw in training to a related word it did not.

questions.stem: What distinguishes the skip-gram and CBOW variants of word2vec?
choices: Skip-gram predicts context words from a target word; CBOW predicts the target word from its context
Skip-gram is supervised and CBOW is not
CBOW handles subwords and skip-gram does not
They differ only in vector size
questions.explanation: The two invert the same prediction task. Skip-gram, predicting context from a target, gives more training signal per occurrence and tends to work better for rare words; CBOW predicts the target from surrounding words and trains faster. Both learn embeddings as a side effect of the task.

questions.stem: In PyTorch, what does nn.EmbeddingBag do that nn.Embedding does not?
choices: It supports larger vocabularies
It looks up and aggregates a bag of embeddings in one operation, avoiding materialising the intermediate per-token tensor
It trains without gradients
It normalises the vectors
questions.explanation: EmbeddingBag fuses lookup and reduction — mean, sum or max — over a sequence of indices. For bag-style models it is faster and more memory-efficient than an Embedding followed by a separate aggregation, because the per-token tensor is never built.

questions.stem: What does an N-gram language model estimate?
choices: The probability of the next word given the previous N-1 words
The number of distinct words in a document
The sentiment of a sentence
The translation of a phrase
questions.explanation: An N-gram model makes a Markov assumption: the next word depends only on a fixed window of preceding words. That makes it easy to estimate by counting, and fundamentally unable to capture dependencies longer than the window — the limitation neural language models address.

questions.stem: Which TWO problems limit recurrent neural networks on long sequences?
choices: Gradients vanish or explode as they are propagated back through many time steps
Computation is inherently sequential, so time steps cannot be parallelised during training
They cannot represent word embeddings
They require labelled data at every time step
questions.explanation: Both limits motivated the transformer. Long gradient paths make distant dependencies hard to learn, and the recurrence forces step-by-step computation that no amount of hardware can parallelise. Attention replaces recurrence with a direct connection between all positions, computed in parallel.

questions.stem: How do LSTM and GRU cells improve on a plain RNN?
choices: They remove the recurrence entirely
They add gating that controls what is kept, forgotten and output, giving gradients a shorter path across time
They process sequences in parallel
They eliminate the need for embeddings
questions.explanation: Gates let the cell carry information across many steps without repeatedly multiplying it, which mitigates vanishing gradients. They ease the memory problem but keep the sequential bottleneck, so they remain slower to train than attention-based models.

questions.stem: In a sequence-to-sequence model, what does the encoder produce?
choices: The output sequence directly
A representation of the input sequence that the decoder conditions on when generating output
The loss value
The vocabulary
questions.explanation: The encoder compresses the source into a representation; the decoder generates the target one token at a time, conditioned on that representation and on what it has already produced. Forcing everything through a single fixed vector was the bottleneck that attention removed.

questions.stem: What is teacher forcing during sequence model training?
choices: Training on a teacher model's outputs instead of real data
Feeding the ground-truth previous token as input at each step rather than the model's own prediction
Freezing the encoder while training the decoder
Using a larger learning rate early in training
questions.explanation: Teacher forcing keeps training on the correct trajectory and converges much faster, but it creates exposure bias: at inference the model must consume its own outputs, including its mistakes, a condition it never trained under. Training on a teacher model's outputs is knowledge distillation, a different technique.

questions.stem: What does perplexity measure for a language model?
choices: How fast the model generates text
How surprised the model is by the held-out text — lower perplexity means it assigned higher probability to what actually occurred
How many parameters it has
How diverse its outputs are
questions.explanation: Perplexity is the exponentiated average negative log-likelihood of held-out text, interpretable as the effective number of equally likely choices at each step. It measures modelling of the distribution, not usefulness — a low-perplexity model can still be unhelpful or untruthful.

questions.stem: What does BLEU score compare?
choices: Model size against accuracy
N-gram overlap between generated text and one or more reference texts
Training loss against validation loss
Token count against latency
questions.explanation: BLEU measures precision of overlapping n-grams against references, with a brevity penalty. It was designed for machine translation and rewards surface agreement, so it penalises a correct paraphrase that uses different words — a known weakness for open-ended generation.

questions.stem: Why can BLEU and ROUGE be misleading for evaluating a summarisation model?
choices: They only work on translation
They reward surface overlap with the reference, so a faithful summary phrased differently scores poorly while a fluent but inaccurate one reusing reference wording can score well
They require a GPU
They cannot handle documents over 1,000 words
questions.explanation: Both metrics are proxies for agreement with a reference, not for correctness or usefulness. A valid summary that paraphrases is punished, and copying reference vocabulary is rewarded regardless of meaning. That gap is why semantic metrics and human or model-based judgement supplement them.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a softmax layer at the output of a language model?
choices: To reduce the vocabulary
To convert raw scores over the vocabulary into a probability distribution summing to one
To mask padding tokens
To compute the gradient
questions.explanation: Softmax exponentiates and normalises the logits so they can be read as probabilities over the next token, which is what sampling and cross-entropy loss both require. Temperature acts by scaling the logits before this step.

questions.stem: What loss function is standard for training a language model to predict the next token?
choices: Mean squared error
Cross-entropy loss between the predicted distribution and the actual next token
Hinge loss
Cosine similarity
questions.explanation: Next-token prediction is classification over the vocabulary, so cross-entropy is the natural loss: it penalises assigning low probability to the token that actually occurred. Mean squared error suits regression, and hinge loss suits margin-based classifiers.

questions.stem: Which TWO are true of pretrained embeddings such as word2vec or GloVe compared with contextual embeddings from BERT?
choices: They assign one fixed vector per word regardless of the sentence it appears in
They cannot distinguish the two senses of a word like 'bank'
They are computed fresh for each occurrence
They require the whole sentence as input
questions.explanation: Static embeddings are a lookup table: one vector per word type, so every sense collapses into a single point. Contextual models compute a different vector for each occurrence based on surrounding text, which is precisely what resolves polysemy.

questions.stem: A classifier trained on embeddings performs well on common words and poorly on rare ones. What is the likely cause?
choices: The learning rate is too low
Rare words have few occurrences, so their embeddings are poorly estimated; subword representations or pooling with frequent neighbours help
The model has too many layers
The batch size is too large
questions.explanation: An embedding is learned from the contexts a word appears in, so words seen a handful of times get vectors little better than noise. Subword units let rare words inherit meaning from familiar fragments, which is one reason modern tokenisers are subword-based.

questions.stem: What does it mean that a language model is autoregressive?
choices: It regresses to the mean of the training data
It generates each token conditioned on the tokens it has already produced
It trains on its own outputs
It predicts all tokens simultaneously
questions.explanation: Autoregressive generation feeds each produced token back as input for the next, which is why output is inherently sequential and why generating N tokens costs roughly N forward passes. Training on one's own outputs is a separate idea, and simultaneous prediction describes non-autoregressive models.

questions.stem: Why is a validation set used during training rather than only at the end?
choices: To increase the training data
To detect the point at which the model begins to overfit, so training can stop or hyperparameters be adjusted
To compute the gradients
To shuffle the data
questions.explanation: Watching held-out loss during training reveals the divergence point where training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises — the signature of memorisation. Early stopping uses exactly this signal. Gradients come only from the training set.

questions.stem: Beam search with a wide beam sometimes produces worse translations than a narrow beam. What explains this?
choices: Wider beams are computationally unstable
Wider search finds higher-probability sequences, and very high-probability output under the model tends toward short, generic text — the model's objective and output quality are not perfectly aligned
The beam width must equal the batch size
Wider beams overflow the context window
questions.explanation: Beam search optimises sequence likelihood, and searching harder finds more of what the model considers likely — which for trained sequence models skews short and bland. Length normalisation and coverage penalties exist to counteract it. It is a clean illustration of a proxy objective diverging from the goal.
